clinicalPearls: An intermediate (rarely metastasising) neoplasm composed of myofibroblastic and fibroblastic spindle cells set within a prominent inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells, lymphocytes and eosinophils
About half of cases harbour rearrangement of the ALK gene, and a subset without ALK involvement carry ROS1, NTRK or other kinase fusions
Most common in children and young adults, with characteristic sites in the lung, mesentery, omentum, retroperitoneum and pelvis
May produce constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, anaemia and raised inflammatory markers that resolve after resection
ALK immunohistochemistry is a useful screening tool, with cytoplasmic staining, and can be confirmed by FISH or molecular testing
The epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma variant, often with nuclear-membrane ALK staining and RANBP2-ALK fusion, is more aggressive
Targeted ALK inhibition (for example crizotinib) is effective in unresectable or metastatic ALK-positive disease
reference.pathophysiology: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour is a clonal neoplasm of myofibroblastic cells, most often driven by a fusion involving the ALK receptor tyrosine kinase that leads to constitutive kinase activation and cell proliferation. In ALK-negative cases, alternative kinase fusions such as those involving ROS1 or NTRK play an equivalent oncogenic role. The characteristic dense inflammatory background of plasma cells and lymphocytes reflects the tumour's biology rather than a reactive process, which historically led to the misleading label of inflammatory pseudotumour.
additionalDifferentials: IgG4-related sclerosing disease and reactive inflammatory pseudotumour
additionalInvestigations: ALK immunohistochemistry as an initial screen for kinase rearrangement
FISH or next-generation sequencing for ALK, ROS1 and NTRK fusions
Immunohistochemistry for smooth muscle actin, desmin and exclusion markers such as CD117, DOG1 and S100
IgG4 and IgG plasma cell studies to distinguish IgG4-related disease
Cross-sectional imaging to define the mass and detect multifocal or metastatic disease
Inflammatory markers and blood count to document paraneoplastic constitutional features
redFlags: Rapid enlargement, local invasion or multifocal intra-abdominal disease
Epithelioid morphology with nuclear-membrane ALK pattern suggesting the aggressive sarcoma variant
Metastatic spread, which although uncommon indicates a worse course
Persistent systemic inflammatory symptoms despite an apparently localised mass
reference.prognosis: Most inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours are cured by complete excision, though local recurrence occurs in a minority and distant metastasis is rare; the epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma variant behaves more aggressively, and ALK inhibition offers durable responses in unresectable or metastatic ALK-positive disease.
pitfalls: Dismissing the lesion as a purely reactive inflammatory pseudotumour and not testing for kinase fusions
Confusing it with IgG4-related disease, which has overlapping histology but different management
Assuming ALK negativity excludes a targetable driver, since ROS1 and NTRK fusions occur
Underestimating the epithelioid variant because of its deceptively inflammatory appearance
Attributing constitutional symptoms to infection rather than the tumour itself
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Thoracic Tumours
management: Achieve complete surgical excision with clear margins as the mainstay of treatment for localised disease
Use ALK-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors (such as crizotinib) for ALK-positive unresectable, recurrent or metastatic tumours
Direct therapy against alternative drivers with ROS1- or NTRK-targeted inhibitors in ALK-negative fusion-positive tumours
Consider neoadjuvant targeted therapy or anti-inflammatory agents to downstage borderline-resectable lesions
Undertake surveillance cross-sectional imaging for local recurrence and, in the aggressive epithelioid variant, for metastatic spread
Manage within a sarcoma multidisciplinary team with surgical oncology and specialist pathology for molecular characterisation
